title: Language Modelling
oneLiner: A language model guesses how likely a sentence is, or which word comes next, by counting which words tend to follow which.

what.html:
A language model gives every possible sentence a probability. "I saw a van" gets a high score; "eyes awe of an" a tiny one. The simplest kind, an n-gram model, just counts how often each word follows the previous one or two words in a large amount of text.

Everyday versionWhen a friend starts "I'll have a cup of…", you already expect "tea" or "coffee". You learned that from hearing thousands of sentences, which is exactly what the counts capture.

why.html:
• Translation, spelling correction, speech recognition and autocomplete all use one to choose the most natural option.
  • It introduces ideas used by every modern chatbot: next-word prediction, smoothing and perplexity.
  • It shows clearly why data is never enough: most word combinations are never seen.

how.title: Picking the fluent option
how.html: Generate a few candidates, then let the language model pick: "high winds tonight", not "large winds tonight".

how.title: One word at a time, short memory
how.html: A sentence's probability is the product of each word's probability given the words before it. Long histories are never seen often enough, so we only look back one or two words (the Markov assumption).

how.title: Count and divide
how.html: P(am | I) = (times "I am" appears) ÷ (times "I" appears). In "I am Sam / Sam I am / I do not like…", that is 2/3.

how.title: Scoring a real sentence
how.html: Multiply the pieces: 0.25 × 0.33 × 0.0011 × 0.5 × 0.68 ≈ 0.000031 for "i want english food". Real systems add logarithms instead, so the numbers don't vanish.

how.title: The zero problem
how.html: A pair never seen in training ("i to", or "denied the offer") gets probability 0, and so does any sentence containing it. Add-1 smoothing pretends every pair was seen once more. It works, but takes too much probability from common pairs: "i want" effectively drops from 827 to 527 counts.

how.title: Fall back on shorter contexts
how.html: If the three-word phrase was never seen, use the two-word or one-word estimate (backoff), or always blend all three with weights that add to 1 (interpolation).

how.title: Words never seen before
how.html: Fix a vocabulary and replace every other word with a special <UNK> token, both in training and at test time, so unknown words still get a sensible probability.

how.title: How surprised is the model?
how.html: Perplexity measures how many equally likely words the model feels it is choosing among. Lower is better: 962 for single words, 170 with one word of context, 109 with two, on newspaper text.

demo.html: Generate sentences from models trained on a handful of restaurant requests. Single-word models produce word salad; two-word models sound locally right; three-word models start copying the training sentences.

example.html:
Perplexity of digits. If each of the ten digits is equally likely, every test digit has probability 1/10, so a string of N digits has probability (1/10)^N and perplexity ((1/10)^N)^(−1/N) = 10: the model is choosing among ten options each time.

Supplementary The best classical method, Kneser–Ney smoothing, asks not just how often a word appears but in how many different contexts: "Francisco" is common but almost always follows "San", so it is a poor guess after a new word.

misunderstandings: Longer n-grams are sparser; without smoothing they overfit.
Add-1 smoothing is the standard for LMs.
It moves too much mass; better methods exist.
Low perplexity guarantees a better application.
It usually helps, but the real test is extrinsic.
takeaways: An LM assigns P(sentence) or P(next word).
Chain rule exactly; Markov assumption approximately.
MLE: count(prev w) ÷ count(prev); use logs.
Zeros break models: add-1 / add-k, backoff, interpolation.
Map unknown words to <UNK>; evaluate with perplexity (lower is better).
thirty: A language model assigns P(w₁…wₙ) = Π P(wₖ | history) or the next-word probability; it ranks candidates in translation, spelling and speech. The Markov assumption keeps only the last n − 1 words (bigram, trigram). MLE estimates P(w | prev) = C(prev w)/C(prev): in the Sam corpus P(I|<s>) = 2/3, P(am|I) = 2/3. On restaurant queries, P(<s> i want english food </s>) = 0.25 × 0.33 × 0.0011 × 0.5 × 0.68 ≈ 0.000031 (computed in log space). Unseen n-grams get zero; add-1 gives (C + 1)/(C(prev) + V), e.g. P(want|i) = 828/3979 = 0.21, reconstituted count 827 → 527. Backoff and interpolation (λs sum to 1, tuned on held-out data) use lower orders; stupid backoff multiplies by 0.4 and returns scores. Unknown words map to <UNK>. Perplexity PP = P(W)^(−1/N) is the average branching factor (digits → 10; unigram 962, bigram 170, trigram 109).
